node.aim.answers: `bearing_deg` is the true bearing between the two positions the scenario already holds, and `gain_dbi` is this node's pattern read along it - which is the part worth reading, because on an omni it is the figure it was before and a control that reports success while changing nothing is one somebody trusts once. Only the named node turns: what the far end hears back still depends on where its own antenna points. Refused where either node is unknown, where a node is aimed at itself, and where both stand at the same position, which has no bearing between them.

example.what: point the hilltop repeater at the node it talks to

node.antenna.what: report what one node's antenna is and which way it points

params.name: node
params.what: the node to ask about

node.antenna.answers: The same words the verb that sets an antenna takes, so what comes back can be handed straight back in. A node carrying no antenna answers with an empty `pattern` and `peak_dbi` zero rather than as an omni at 0 dBi, which in a table of numbers those two would otherwise share. Both gain figures are the peak along boresight; what a given link is actually worth is the pattern read along the bearing to the far end, and differs in each direction.

example.what: ask what a node stands under and where it faces

node.card.what: Report or change what is in one node's card slot: whether a card is fitted, which file it is, and whether to erase it.

params.name: node
params.what: which node

params.name: fitted
params.what: put a card in the slot or take it out; unchanged when absent

params.name: file
params.what: the file behind the card; empty string returns it to the node's own, named after the node and kept beside its flash

params.name: wipe
params.what: erase the card, which is what reformatting one is

node.card.answers: Asking with nothing but a node changes nothing and reports the slot as it stands. `slot` is what the scenario says - fitted, empty or unstated - while `fitted` is whether the node actually has storage, which a firmware that keeps its settings on the card makes true whatever the slot says. `bytes` is nought where the file has not been made yet, which is the normal state before a first run.

example.what: ask what is in a node's card slot

node.energy.what: run a year of sun and battery at one named node, at the duty cycle the run measured for it rather than one typed into a form, for the node window that has a name and no selection to work from

params.name: node
params.what: the node to study; a name this network has not got, or none at all, is refused - and note that the call selects whatever it names and deselects everything else

node.energy.answers: Refused outright unless MESHBENCH_ENERGY is set: the solar model is not trusted yet, and a plausible worst-day figure from an untrusted model is worse than none. The year itself - worst state of charge, the day it falls on, the dead days - goes into the snapshot and onto the status line rather than into this answer. With no run behind it the duty cycle is zero, which sizes the site against a node that never transmits.

example.what: ask whether one repeater's pack survives December

node.output.what: read what a node's serial port, emulator or radio model has printed

params.name: node
params.what: the node to read

params.name: source
params.what: which voice: serial, rom, emulator, radio; serial when absent, and anything else is refused

params.name: lines
params.what: how many lines of the tail to answer with; 200 when absent or not a positive number, and never more than the 2000 the pane itself holds

node.output.answers: `total` is how many lines the file has and `lines` how many the pane was given, so the two differing is a tail rather than a board that stopped talking. `tail` is the shorter answer this call gets, and is empty with a `note` where the source is one this node's backend does not have - a native node has no emulator and no radio log - or where it has not run since the workbench started.

example.what: read the last lines a board printed

node.output_window.what: Open one node's one log in a window of its own, so a board's screen and several of its logs can be watched at once.

params.name: node
params.what: which node

params.name: source
params.what: which log: serial, rom, emulator, radio; serial when absent

node.output_window.answers: The answer says the window was opened, not what is in it: the pane fills from the tick that follows. Refused outright in a headless session, there being no window to open one beside.

example.what: watch the emulator's log beside the board's screen

node.provisioning.what: read the console lines a node is told before a run, so a region defined but never allowed to flood is visible rather than looking like broken radio

params.name: node
params.what: whose script to read; a name this network has not got is refused

node.provisioning.answers: `commands` is the lines that are actually sent, with the commentary dropped; the panel keeps the annotated form, each line with the reason it exists.

example.what: see what a node will be told at start

node.radio.what: ask a running node what frequency, modulation and transmit power it is actually set to, and say where that disagrees with the figures every path loss for it was computed from

params.name: node
params.what: the node to ask; absent falls back to the selected node, and with nothing selected either the call is refused

node.radio.answers: `assumed` and `reported` are both objects of freq_mhz, bandwidth_hz, spreading_factor, coding_rate and tx_dbm. A node answers over a frame or its console and the reply only lands when the engine next steps, so the first call usually returns `reported` null with a `note` saying to ask again. An empty `differences` means the two agree, not that nothing was checked; coding rate is deliberately never compared, because model and firmware write the same setting in different conventions.

example.what: check the model is pricing this node's real transmit power

node.radio_adopt.what: take the radio configuration a node has already reported as the one the model uses for it, so the path losses are computed from what the node transmits with rather than from what the scenario intended

params.name: node
params.what: the node to believe; absent falls back to the selected node, and a node that is not a connected companion, or has not reported yet, is refused with what to do about it

node.radio_adopt.answers: `tx_dbm` is the node's own transmit power, now the model's. Frequency, bandwidth and spreading factor are adopted with it, and because path loss is cached per pair the engine is rebuilt and every link measured again on a worker.

example.what: stop modelling a power this node does not have

node.reflash_failed.what: report that a build change did not go through, which reaches the operator after the caller that asked has already been told it was accepted

params.name: reason
params.what: what went wrong, said to the operator as it stands

node.reflash_failed.answers: Answers with nothing: what it changes is the stats and the status line.

node.reflashed.what: report that a node's build change went through, refreshing the counters and the node's own window, which reads the node list rather than the stats and so showed the old build for ever

params.name: message
params.what: what to say, whose first word is the node that changed

node.reflashed.answers: Answers with nothing: what it changes is the stats, the node list and the status line.

node.set_board.what: say what hardware a node is, which is a change to the physics and not a label: the transmit ceiling, the receive chain's noise figure and the battery the energy model runs on all come off the board

params.name: node
params.what: which node changes hardware; absent or unknown is refused

params.name: board
params.what: the board it is, as the firmware library names one; a board this build has no profile for is refused, and an empty or absent name returns the node to no particular hardware, which is a build for this machine

node.set_board.answers: A build pinned for the old board is cleared rather than carried across, because that image is for that hardware and a node keeping the pin would look configured and refuse at start.

example.what: make a node a Heltec WSL3

node.set_firmware.what: change the build a node runs and apply it now, stopping the node, provisioning it and starting it again, because firmware is chosen when a node launches and nothing else would take effect

params.name: node
params.what: which node changes build; absent, blank or unknown is refused

params.name: version
params.what: the build to run, as the firmware library names it; absent or blank is refused

params.name: board
params.what: the hardware the image is for, because a board image is that image for that board; absent means a build for this machine

params.name: role
params.what: which MeshCore role the image is; absent leaves the node's role as it was

node.set_firmware.answers: The answer says the change was accepted, not that it took: the stop, provision and start run behind it, and a build that will not provision or a node that will not start arrives afterwards as node.reflash_failed.

example.what: put a host build on one node and restart it into it

node.set_firmware_only.what: record the build a node will run at its next start without touching the node now, for setting a fleet up before anything is launched

params.name: node
params.what: which node is set; absent, blank or unknown is refused

params.name: version
params.what: the build it will run, as the firmware library names it; absent or blank is refused

params.name: board
params.what: the hardware the image is for; absent means a build for this machine, and clears any board the node was pinned to

params.name: role
params.what: which MeshCore role the image is; absent leaves the node's role as it was

node.set_firmware_only.answers: Nothing restarts. A node already running goes on running what it has until something stops it, which is the difference between this and node.set_firmware.

example.what: choose what a node will run without disturbing it

node.start.what: bring a stopped node's firmware back up, which goes through the whole-mesh attach and so starts every other stopped node with it

params.name: node
params.what: which node starts; a name this network has not got is refused, and so is a node that is already running

node.start.answers: `started` is the node that was asked for, not everything that came up: the attach behind it skips only the nodes already running.

example.what: put a stopped node back on the air

node.stop.what: take one node's firmware down while leaving the node in the scenario, so it reports its final counters on the way out - which are usually the only evidence about a node that was misbehaving

params.name: node
params.what: which node stops; a name this network has not got is refused, and so is a node that is not running firmware

example.what: take one node off the air

node.truerf.what: give one receiver waveform verdicts inside a calculated run, so the pair being studied is decided by the full receive chain while the rest of the network stays on the fast model

params.name: node
params.what: the receiver that takes waveform verdicts; a name no node has is refused rather than ignored

params.name: on
params.what: true to hold this node on waveform whatever the run mode; absent means false, which puts it back on the run's own mode

example.what: decide this one receiver honestly, at one node's cost

node.window.what: Open one node's own window, the thing people put on a second monitor.

params.name: node
params.what: which node

params.name: tab
params.what: which tab to open on; the window's default when absent

node.window.answers: `tab` is the tab the window actually opened on, which is not always the one asked for. Refused outright in a headless session, there being no window to open one beside.

example.what: put one node on a second monitor

node.wipe.what: erase one node's stored state: its flash, its card and its files

params.name: node
params.what: the node to put back to factory

params.name: confirm
params.what: false lists what would go and removes nothing; absent or true erases it

node.wipe.answers: `wiped` counts what went and `removed` names it, the node's card included where it keeps one elsewhere; the emulator's own sockets are left, being recreated at the next start. With `confirm` false nothing is touched and `would_remove` names what a wipe would take. A node with nothing on disk answers zero rather than refusing. Refused where the node is not an emulated board, where it is still running, and where only part of it could be removed - a partial wipe is an error naming what stayed, because a board that boots back into settings said to be gone is worse than one that was never wiped.

example.what: see what putting a board back to factory would take

nodes.add_to_selection.what: add nodes to whatever is already selected, which is the shift-drag, and the way a selection is built up out of several passes over the map

params.name: names
params.what: the nodes to add, as a list, one name, or {"names": [...]}; a name this network has not got refuses the whole call, and no names at all adds nothing and leaves the selection as it was

nodes.add_to_selection.answers: `added` counts the nodes matched, not the nodes newly selected: one that was already in the selection is counted again.

example.what: add one more node to the selection

nodes.allow_flood.what: let a node forward a flood whatever region it was scoped to, which is the difference between a scenario that relays and one that transmits everything, relays nothing and reports no error

params.name: on
params.what: true to forward any flood, false to forward only the scoped ones; anything that is not a boolean leaves it true

params.name: node
params.what: the one node to set, matched on the whole name; absent, every node is set, and a name that matches nothing sets nothing and is not refused

nodes.allow_flood.answers: `nodes` is how many were written to, which is 0 when the name matched nothing.

example.what: let every node forward a flood whatever its scope

nodes.antenna.what: choose and aim the antenna on one node, on a kind, or on every node

params.name: node
params.what: one node; absent means every node the other filters leave

params.name: kind
params.what: only nodes of this scenario kind

params.name: pattern
params.what: isotropic, dipole, collinear or yagi

params.name: gain_dbi_peak
params.what: the headline gain, for a collinear or a yagi

params.name: beamwidth_deg
params.what: a yagi's horizontal half-power beamwidth

params.name: front_to_back_db
params.what: how far down a yagi's back is on its front

params.name: bearing_deg
params.what: compass bearing of boresight, 0 at north

params.name: downtilt_deg
params.what: degrees the beam is tilted below the horizon

params.name: polarisation
params.what: vertical, horizontal or circular

params.name: feedline_db
params.what: cable and connector loss, as a positive number

nodes.antenna.answers: What the last matched node now carries, with `nodes` for how many were changed and no node name, because the answer is about a selection rather than one node. Each field named replaces one part of the antenna already there, so a collinear switched to a yagi keeps the gain figure somebody chose. Setting one rebuilds the engine over the changed nodes and re-measures every link: the cached look angles belong to the antenna that used to be there. Refused where a named node is unknown, where a pattern or a polarisation is not one the model prices, and where the filters leave no node at all.

example.what: stand a yagi on the hill, facing down the Forth

nodes.delete.what: take one node out of the scenario for good, which is how an imported deployment is cut down to what a desktop will actually run

params.name: node
params.what: the node to remove, matched on the whole name and exactly; an empty one is refused, and so is a name no node has, rather than deleting nothing quietly

nodes.delete.answers: `nodes` is how many are left. It rebuilds the engine and empties the link matrix, so every remaining pair is measured again as a job before the run means anything.

example.what: drop a node from the scenario

nodes.delete_many.what: remove a set of nodes in one rebuild, rather than one call each rebuilding the scenario and cancelling the warm the last one started

params.name: nodes
params.what: the names to remove; one this network has not got refuses the whole call and removes nothing, and naming none is accepted and does nothing

nodes.delete_many.answers: `deleted` is the names that went and `nodes` is how many are left. Every link is dropped and the matrix re-measured behind the answer, because the network is not the one that was measured.

example.what: take one node out of the network

nodes.keep.what: cut a network down to the nodes named and remove everything else, which is how trimming a fixture is actually said

params.name: nodes
params.what: the names to keep; one this network has not got refuses the whole call and removes nothing, and naming none keeps nothing, which empties the network

nodes.keep.answers: `deleted` names what was removed rather than what was kept, and `nodes` is how many are left.

example.what: cut a network down to one node

nodes.list.what: read back the whole network as it stands, which is what anything automated does first and the only way to see what a scenario built by a script actually got
nodes.list.answers: A row per node under `nodes` and `count` beside them, so a caller need not measure the list to know how big the network is. Each row carries two boards, which are two facts: `board` is what the node is and `firmware_board` what its image was built for, and they come apart the moment a host build is pointed at a T-Deck. There is no limit and no paging, so an imported deployment answers with all of it.

example.what: see what is in the scenario

nodes.move.what: put a node at a position and move its physics with its marker, forgetting the losses cached for it so the next window an attached SDR client hears is the one from where it now stands

params.name: name
params.what: which node moves; absent, blank or unknown is refused

params.name: lat
params.what: degrees north, minus 90 to 90; absent or outside that is refused rather than read as nought, which used to put the node in the Gulf of Guinea and report it as asked for

params.name: lon
params.what: degrees east, minus 180 to 180; absent or outside that is refused

example.what: move a node onto the hill it is named after

nodes.near.what: order the rest of the network by how far it is from one node, which is how an imported deployment is cut down to a neighbourhood a desktop will actually run

params.name: node
params.what: the node to measure from, matched as nodes elsewhere are matched; a name no node has is refused, and so is an absent one

params.name: count
params.what: how many of the nearest to return; anything not a positive number returns every other node in the scenario

nodes.near.answers: `node` is the name as the scenario spells it. `near` is a row per other node with its great-circle distance in `km`, nearest first, ties broken on the name. The distance is the same geometry the path losses are computed on, so a script's idea of nearest and the simulator's are one idea; it is still only a distance, and says nothing about whether either end can hear the other.

example.what: find the neighbourhood around a repeater

nodes.place.what: put one node down at a position, which is how a repeater a feed never carried gets into a scenario, and how a mesh is built by hand rather than imported

params.name: name
params.what: what the node is called, which has to be new: a name the network already holds is refused rather than merged

params.name: lat
params.what: latitude in degrees; the call is refused without it

params.name: lon
params.what: longitude in degrees; the call is refused without it

params.name: kind
params.what: what the node is - simple-repeater, advanced-repeater, companion, room-server, sdr-observer or emitter; absent places a simple-repeater

params.name: board
params.what: the hardware it is, which decides the transmit ceiling, the receive chain's noise figure, the battery and the antenna it stands under; a name no board profile has is refused rather than defaulted to a plausible one, and absent leaves it unstated

params.name: height_m
params.what: antenna height above ground in metres; absent is 10

params.name: tx_dbm
params.what: transmit power in decibel-milliwatts; absent is 22

nodes.place.answers: `regions` and the firmware build are inherited from the neighbours rather than left empty: a node holding a region its neighbours do not is as silent as one holding none. `nodes` is the whole network's count afterwards. The links are not in the answer, because measuring them is a worker's job and this returns before it.

example.what: put a repeater on the hill and see what it wins

nodes.regions.what: say which regions a node holds, which is how a node placed by hand is given what its neighbours already hold: inference reads the real network's traffic and so reaches only the nodes that were seen on it

params.name: node
params.what: the one node to set, matched on the whole name; absent, every node in the scenario is set, and a name that matches nothing sets nothing and is not refused

params.name: regions
params.what: the regions the node is to hold, as strings; absent or not a list of strings leaves the node holding none, which is a clear rather than a call that did nothing

nodes.regions.answers: `nodes` is how many were written to, which is 0 when the name matched nothing. What is given replaces what a node held rather than adding to it.

example.what: give a hand-placed repeater the region its neighbours use

nodes.search.what: find a node by roughly what it is called and rank the matches, so a name full of emoji, box-drawing characters or Gaelic accents can be reached by something a person can type

params.name: query
params.what: roughly the name, with accents and emoji ignored on both sides; one with no letters or digits in it is refused rather than answered with the whole network

params.name: limit
params.what: how many of the best matches to return; anything not a positive number leaves it at ten

nodes.search.answers: `total` is how many names scored well enough to be offered and `matches` only the best of them, so the two differ whenever the limit bit. Each match carries a score from 0.2 to 1, where 1 is the same name; a shorter name beats a longer one that matched the same way, and ties break on the name so the same query answers the same way twice. No match at all is an empty list, not an error.

example.what: find a node whose real name cannot be typed

nodes.select.what: make one node the selection, which is what the verbs that act on "the selected node" - sim.inject among them - go on to find

params.name: node
params.what: which node; a name this network has not got is not refused here, and clears the selection, as an empty name does

nodes.select.answers: `selected` is the name that was asked for, whether or not a node answers to it: this is the click a map sends, and it sets every node's selected flag from that one name.

example.what: select one node

nodes.select_many.what: replace the selection with a set of nodes, which is what a box drag on the map amounts to and what a script does before any verb that acts on a selection

params.name: names
params.what: the nodes to select, as a list, one name, or {"names": [...]}; a name this network has not got refuses the whole call, and no names at all clears the selection

nodes.select_many.answers: Every other node is deselected, so this is a replacement rather than an addition; nodes.add_to_selection is the addition.

example.what: select two nodes at once

nodes.stats.what: recompute every node's counters now rather than at the next tick, and answer with the rows themselves, which is how anything outside the window asks whether a node is running
nodes.stats.answers: `nodes` is how many rows there are and `stats` is the rows. A session with no engine built has no counters to report and answers with none, which is not a failure.

example.what: read every node's state and counters

packet.close.what: put the open packet away, which is also what stops the per-tick rebuild that keeps an open one live
packet.close.answers: Nothing comes back, whether or not a packet was open: the answer is null and the call cannot fail.

example.what: stop following a packet

packet.open.what: dissect one transmission and gather what every node did with it, and leave it as the packet the view keeps following while its message is still spreading

params.name: id
params.what: the transmission's id; absent or zero is refused

params.name: seek
params.what: step this many ids at a time until a transmission that is still in the ledger is found, up to fifty tries, which is what the previous and next arrows send; absent means take the given id or nothing

packet.open.answers: `id` is the transmission actually opened, which is not the one asked for when `seek` walked to a neighbouring one. `transmissions` counts every time the message was put on the air, so a relayed flood is told from a single advert without reading the header, and `reached` is how many distinct nodes heard any of them. Refused where no engine is built, and where nothing of that id is left in the event log.

example.what: open the first transmission of a run

panel.close.what: take a panel out of the layout, giving the room to what is left

params.name: name
params.what: the panel to close; an unknown or missing name is refused with the list of the ones there are

panel.close.answers: Whether the panel was open is not asked, only whether it exists: closing one that is not in the layout answers the same way and does nothing, which is what the caller wanted anyway. Refuses when no interface is attached.

example.what: clear the rail before a screenshot

panel.dock.what: bring a popped-out panel back into the main window, which is the other half of panel.pop_out and the only way back for a window a compositor has hidden

params.name: name
params.what: the panel to dock; an unknown or missing name is refused with the list of the ones there are

panel.dock.answers: `where` is always "layout". A panel that was never popped out is docked where it belongs rather than refused. Refuses when no interface is attached.

example.what: put the map back in the main window

panel.open.what: put a panel in the layout, switching to the view it belongs to on the way, which is how the panels no view starts with are reached at all

params.name: name
params.what: the panel, spelled as panels.list spells it; an unknown or missing name is refused with the list of the ones there are

panel.open.answers: It answers once the panel has been asked for, not once it is drawn: the layout is the frame loop's, and the change lands on the next frame. A panel already in the layout is left where it is. Refuses when no interface is attached.

example.what: bring up the waterfall from a script

panel.pop_out.what: send a panel out into a window of its own, so a second monitor can hold what the layout has no room for

params.name: name
params.what: the panel to pop out; an unknown or missing name is refused with the list of the ones there are

panel.pop_out.answers: `where` is always "window", the verb having only one destination: it is there so an answer read on its own says what happened. Refuses when no interface is attached.

example.what: give the map a monitor to itself

panels.list.what: Name every panel the interface has registered.
panels.list.answers: Every panel that exists, sorted, not the ones on screen: a panel nothing has opened is still named here, which is what makes this the list to choose a `panel.open` from. Refuses when no interface is attached.

example.what: find out what there is to open

plan.failed.what: put a route search's error in the status line, which is the only place it can go: the search runs on a worker, long after the verb that started it answered
plan.failed.answers: Nothing. It exists to say something to the operator.

plan.routes.what: search for the paths a message could take between the first and last selected nodes, on a worker, and answer with only the pair it has gone off to search between
plan.routes.answers: It takes its ends from the selection rather than from parameters, and refuses where fewer than two nodes are selected. The routes themselves arrive later through an internal callback and land on the world; nothing here waits for them, and a search that fails says so in the status line rather than in this answer.

example.what: why a message gets from one end to the other

plan.set.what: take a finished route search onto the world, which is the only place the paths become something the map can draw
plan.set.answers: Anything that is not a []state.Route leaves the world holding no routes rather than being refused, so a caller from outside the process would silently erase them - which is why the socket is not allowed to reach it.

project.list.what: name everything that can be opened: what project.save has written, where it writes them, and the networks that shipped with this copy
project.list.answers: `projects` is the user's own saved networks, by name, and `dir` is the directory they are read from - always said, whether or not it exists yet, since a caller building a path needs it either way. `fixtures` is the shipped networks, named as the files name them (`fixture-fife-strict`), found on disk beside an install and inside the binary; they are listed rather than copied into the projects directory, so a later release can correct one without overwriting somebody's edit. On a machine that has never run MeshBench `projects` is empty and `fixtures` is not, which is the first-run case and not a fault. A name from `fixtures` is opened by passing it to project.open as it stands; a saved project is opened by joining `dir` and `<name>.json`.

example.what: see what can be opened

project.new.what: throw away what is loaded and start on an empty network, through the same path an open takes, optionally putting the map and the study area on a named place so the first node has somewhere to go

params.name: place
params.what: somewhere to start, looked up the way a study area is, so "Fife" means the same thing here as in the Import panel; empty leaves the map where it was, and a name nothing can be found for is said in the status line rather than refused

project.new.answers: `nodes` is always zero, and `place` appears only where one was named. A run that was going is stopped first, and the firmware behind it with it, since both belonged to the network being discarded. The lookup runs on a worker, so the map and the study area move after this has already answered.

example.what: an empty network to place nodes on by hand

project.open.what: load a fixture and put the camera on what it holds, on the open rather than at the first play, so nobody is left reading a blank map with a node count beside it

params.name: path
params.what: the fixture's path; one that will not load is refused and the session keeps whatever it already had

project.open.answers: `links` is zero on every open, because the matrix is cleared here and re-measured as the job `links`: a path loss over real terrain is minutes of work, so the map draws proximity links until it finishes. A run that was going is stopped first and the status line says so: the clock steps whichever engine is live, and this replaces it and stops the firmware processes behind it, so a script that opens a network mid-run plays again itself once it is ready. Nothing else moves the camera on an open, so a script that wants to be somewhere else says so afterwards with map.centre.

example.what: open a network that ships with the build

project.save.what: write the nodes as they stand, and the margin they are judged against, into a named file under the user's config directory, so the setup can be opened again

params.name: name
params.what: what to call it: a name and not a path, since it is joined onto the projects directory and written to, so a separator or a leading dot is refused rather than followed

project.save.answers: It writes the scenario's nodes only. A run, its capture and the terrain cache are not in the file, so opening it again gives back the network rather than the session.

example.what: keep this network to come back to

provisioning.apply.what: type the current settings into the nodes that are already running, which is the difference between changing what a future run does and changing what this one is doing
provisioning.apply.answers: `nodes` counts the ones that had firmware up and were typed at; a node not running is passed over rather than refused, so a count below the size of the network is normal on a mesh that is still coming up. The commands are queued at each node's serial input, so the clock has to move before the firmware acts on them. A node whose console will not take a line ends the whole call with an error naming it, leaving the nodes after it untouched.

example.what: push changed settings into a mesh that is up

provisioning.get.what: read the switches every node is told at boot, which is what decides whether a mesh comes up named, positioned and in the same conversation as the rest
provisioning.get.answers: The settings themselves, unwrapped. A zero or an empty string is not a value sent to the firmware but a firmware default left alone, and `path_hash_mode` and `comp_path_hash_mode` say the same thing with -1.

example.what: read what the next start will send

provisioning.set.what: change what a future run tells its nodes, a switch at a time, leaving every setting not named where it was

params.name: set_name
params.what: send each node its scenario name; absent leaves it alone, and off leaves a node reporting as its board type

params.name: set_position
params.what: send each node its latitude and longitude; absent leaves it alone, and off leaves a node advertising no position

params.name: set_clock
params.what: set every node to the run's own epoch; absent leaves it alone, and off leaves clocks that reject traffic as replays

params.name: region_from_area
params.what: define a transport region named after the study area; absent leaves it alone

params.name: default_scope
params.what: make that region the one nodes originate under; absent leaves it alone, and off leaves them relaying but never originating

params.name: advert_hops
params.what: how far an advert may flood; absent leaves it alone and zero says nothing to the firmware

params.name: advert_minutes
params.what: how often a node says it is there; absent leaves it alone, zero means never, and anything outside 60 to 240 is clamped into that range because the firmware refuses the rest

params.name: stagger_ms
params.what: milliseconds between node starts; absent leaves it alone

params.name: flood_max_advert
params.what: how far an advert is relayed; absent leaves it alone and zero leaves the firmware's own limit

params.name: path_hash_mode
params.what: the repeaters' path-hash mode; absent leaves it alone and negative says nothing to the firmware

params.name: comp_path_hash_mode
params.what: the companions' own, which is a different question from the repeaters'; absent leaves it alone and negative falls back to path_hash_mode

params.name: loop_detect
params.what: the firmware's loop-detect setting, sent only to nodes that transmit; absent or empty leaves it alone

params.name: cad
params.what: the firmware's CAD mode, sent only to nodes that transmit; absent or empty leaves it alone

params.name: extra
params.what: further console lines, one per line, sent after the rest and unchecked; absent or empty leaves it alone

provisioning.set.answers: Every setting comes back, the same shape as `provisioning.get`, so one call both changes and reads. Nothing reaches a node that is already running: this is what the next start sends, and `provisioning.apply` is what changes a mesh that is up.

example.what: make the mesh advertise, and let adverts cross a country

radio.preset.what: put the nodes on one of the community's agreed modem settings, which decides sensitivity and airtime and therefore every number downstream of them, or list the settings there are to choose from

params.name: preset
params.what: the preset's label, exactly as it is listed; a label no preset has is refused, and absent lists the labels instead of changing anything

params.name: node
params.what: one node to move, named rather than passed bare; absent moves every node in the network

radio.preset.answers: `nodes` is how many were moved, and zero is the answer where `node` named nobody. Called with no preset at all it answers instead with `presets`, the labels available. The frequency is part of a preset, so a change rebuilds the engine and remeasures every link on a worker.

example.what: put the whole network on the settings its neighbours use

resource.fetch.what: download one runtime resource as a job that can be stopped, which is how a headless machine gets the SoftDevice or the emulator toolchain an emulated board is blocked on

params.name: name
params.what: the row's name as resource.list gives it; absent is refused, and so is a name the chosen provider does not hold

params.name: kind
params.what: which provider owns it - softdevice, toolchain, terrain, basemap or buildings - named rather than bare; absent means softdevice, so a row of another kind is not found without it

params.name: version
params.what: the release to fetch, named rather than bare; the row's own version overrides it wherever the row carries one

resource.fetch.answers: It answers as soon as the download is started, not when it has arrived. Progress is the job `resource:<name>`, which `job.list` shows and `job.cancel` stops, and how it ended is said aloud rather than returned here. A resource that fills itself as the map is used is refused: there is nothing to ask for out of context.

example.what: fetch the SoftDevice an emulated nRF52 boots

resource.fetched.what: take a finished download back onto the store's goroutine: say once that it is cached and where its terms are, then relist what is on disk

params.name: name
params.what: the resource that arrived

params.name: version
params.what: the release that arrived, for the sentence it says

resource.licence.what: read the terms a cached resource arrived under, and leave them open in the snapshot for the interface to show

params.name: name
params.what: the row's name; absent or unknown to the chosen provider is refused

params.name: kind
params.what: which provider owns it, named rather than bare; absent means softdevice

params.name: version
params.what: the release whose terms to read, named rather than bare; the row's own version overrides it where it has one

resource.licence.answers: The whole licence text, and the same text is put into the snapshot until `resource.licence.hide` clears it. Refused where the resource is not cached: the terms are a file fetched beside it, not a string this build carries.

example.what: read the terms the SoftDevice came under

resource.licence.hide.what: clear the terms resource.licence left open, so the interface stops showing them
resource.licence.hide.answers: `hidden` is always true. Calling it with nothing open is not an error, and it is left out of the session journal because it changes a window rather than the world.

example.what: put the terms away

resource.list.what: say what this machine already holds of everything downloaded at runtime, what it has cost the disk, and what could still be fetched
resource.list.answers: `rows` is a count, kept for the callers that were already reading it; `resources` is the rows themselves, each carrying its kind, name, version, state, size and path, why it is in the state it is in, and whether it can be fetched, carries terms, or fills itself as the map is used. A provider whose directory cannot be read contributes one row saying so rather than emptying the list.

example.what: see what this machine already holds

resource.remove.what: delete one cached resource from the disk, through whichever provider owns it, and relist what is left

params.name: name
params.what: the row's name; absent is refused, and so is a name the chosen provider does not hold

params.name: kind
params.what: which provider owns it, named rather than bare; absent means softdevice, so removing terrain or a toolchain needs it

params.name: version
params.what: the release to remove, named rather than bare; used only where the row carries no version of its own

resource.remove.answers: Nothing is confirmed here: this deletes, and the asking belongs to whatever called it. Removing 7 GB of terrain and removing a SoftDevice are the same call with a different kind.

example.what: give the terrain cache's disk back

rf.environment.what: point the session at a directory of environment tiles so both RF modes price buildings into the path budget, or take it away again and go back to bare earth

params.name: dir
params.what: the tile directory, as tools/envgen or environ.fetch wrote it; absent is refused unless on is false, because a switch with nothing to switch on would silently leave the model bare

params.name: on
params.what: false drops the environment and returns the model to bare earth; absent or true expects a dir

rf.environment.answers: `environment` is the directory now in force, and empty means bare earth. Every path loss already cached was priced without buildings, so a live engine drops its link cache and the links are measured again.

example.what: charge the paths for the buildings they cross

rf.excess_loss.what: add a flat calibration loss to every path, which is where the clutter, body loss and multipath the bare-earth model has no term for get paid for, and read back what the model is running with

params.name: db
params.what: decibels of loss on top of the modelled path, fitted from observations the study has already validated against; a negative figure would add signal and is refused, and absent changes nothing and only reports, leaving the default zero that makes every margin a best case

rf.excess_loss.answers: `links` is how many links the world is holding as this returns. Path loss is cached per pair for the life of an engine, so setting `db` over a loaded network rebuilds the engine and measures every pair again on a worker: the links are empty until that finishes, and this answers before it does.

example.what: charge the 8 dB a validation run found the model was short

rf.mode.what: choose which physics decides reception, and stamp the choice into the world so every snapshot, saved run and export says which of the two models produced it

params.name: mode
params.what: calculated for link budgets against demodulator floors, which is the fast model, or waveform for the full receive chain of demodulation, FEC and CRC; any other value is refused, and so is the empty string a caller who named nothing sends

example.what: let the receive chain decide, rather than a link budget

rf.realism.what: price in the imperfections the channel otherwise leaves out - crystal error, a delayed echo, fading, receiver implementation loss and front-end clipping - because with all five at zero the model is kinder than the air and every margin it reports is a best case

params.name: osc_ppm
params.what: worst-case crystal error in parts per million, each node offset deterministically within it; absent leaves the current value alone, and zero is a pair of perfect oscillators

params.name: multipath_db
params.what: how far below the direct ray one delayed reflection arrives, in decibels; absent leaves it alone, and zero is a single clean path with nothing to cancel against

params.name: fading_hz
params.what: how fast that echo's phase rotates over simulated time, so a marginal link breathes; absent leaves it alone, and zero holds the interference pattern still

params.name: impl_loss_db
params.what: the receiver's shortfall from theory, applied as extra receiver noise; absent leaves it alone, and zero credits the receiver with its datasheet floor and nothing worse

params.name: saturation_dbm
params.what: the level above which the front end clips, harmonics and all; absent leaves it alone, and zero models a receiver that never overloads however close the transmitter is

rf.realism.answers: `realism` is the whole switch set after the call, including the switches this call did not name, so one knob can move without restating the rest. The effects act on the waveform paths, so a calculated run stores them and shows no change until the physics is switched.

example.what: charge the receiver a realistic 2 dB and let the crystals disagree

rf.toggle.what: flip to whichever RF physics is not running, for a control that is one button rather than a choice of two
rf.toggle.answers: `mode` is the physics now in force, not the one it left.

example.what: swap the physics for the other one

run.save.what: file the counters as they stand as a named run, so two configurations measured an hour apart can still be put side by side

params.name: name
params.what: what to file it under; empty files it as "run", and the time is appended either way so two saves of one name both survive

run.save.answers: It writes into the user's cache directory, not the working directory, and takes its numbers from the renderer's snapshot rather than the world, so what is recorded is what was on screen when it was asked for.

example.what: keep the run to compare the next one against

schedule.add.what: have a node originate traffic on its own at a stated moment of simulated time, so a run reproduces without anybody watching it for the moment to press send

params.name: node
params.what: the node that sends; absent is refused, and so is a name no node in this network carries

params.name: at_ms
params.what: the simulated instant of the first send; absent is zero, which is the start of the run

params.name: every_ms
params.what: repeat interval in simulated milliseconds; absent or zero sends once

params.name: command
params.what: what the node is told to do, in its own console's words; has to be named rather than passed bare, and absent leaves it empty

schedule.add.answers: `sends` is how many the schedule now holds, not the one just added.

example.what: one flood thirty seconds into the run

schedule.clear.what: empty the schedule, which is what editing it amounts to: nothing removes a single send, so a schedule is rebuilt rather than amended

example.what: start the schedule again

sdr.serve.what: offer what one node's antenna hears as an rtl_tcp source, so real SDR software can be pointed at the simulated spectrum rather than at a drawing of it

params.name: node
params.what: the node whose antenna is served; refused when it is absent, not in the scenario, or not in the engine

sdr.serve.answers: `rate_hz` is the node's own receiver bandwidth, one sample per hertz, and 250 kHz where the scenario states none. It is what the stream is rendered at, not what a client is held to: the client's own rate setting is followed. Serving a node already served replaces the listener. The IQ is signal only, with the noise floor added at the server, so a paused run streams a bare floor rather than stopping.

example.what: point SDR software at a node's antenna

sdr.stop.what: close a node's rtl_tcp listener and stop rendering its IQ, which is work a run keeps doing for as long as it is served

params.name: node
params.what: the served node; refused when it is absent or not being served, so a stop is never mistaken for having worked

sdr.stop.answers: Any client on the line is cut rather than told, the same way unplugging a dongle would.

example.what: stop serving a node's antenna

session.checkpoint.what: freeze the whole session to a named checkpoint

params.name: name
params.what: what to call this checkpoint

session.checkpoint.answers: `path` is the file it wrote, in the checkpoints directory under the user's configuration directory. The filename is the name with everything but letters, digits, underscore and hyphen replaced, so two names differing only in punctuation are one file and the second overwrites the first. Refused where there is no network to freeze, and where the name leaves nothing usable behind.

example.what: keep this moment to come back to

session.checkpoints.what: list the checkpoints that can be restored
session.checkpoints.answers: The filenames, sorted, in the form `session.restore` takes as its name - which is the sanitised form rather than the name it was saved under, where the two differ. A machine that has never saved one answers with an empty list rather than an error.

example.what: see what can be gone back to

session.describe.what: the cheapest question a client can ask, and the one worth asking first: whether there is a network in this session at all, and whether its clock is moving
session.describe.answers: Four facts and no more. `now_ms` is simulated time, not wall time, and stands still while `playing` is false. It never fails, so it is also the handshake for a socket that has just connected.

example.what: check what is loaded before driving it

session.journal.what: every command this workbench has been driven with, newest last, and when the process started - so a session picked up cold can be told how the world got here, and whether it has been restarted
session.journal.answers: Each entry is a sequence number, a wall-clock time, the verb, how many nodes there were when it ran, a short rendering of its argument, and the error where it was refused, because a refusal is part of how a session got here. The polls, the interface-only verbs and the workers' own callbacks are left out, and only the last few hundred commands are kept. `started_ms` is when this process started, which is how a driver tells the session it has been talking to all along from one that has been restarted under it.

example.what: ask how this session got here

session.list.what: list the workbenches running on this machine, this one included

example.what: which workbenches are up, and what each is holding

session.restore.what: rebuild a checkpoint and replay to the moment it was taken

params.name: name
params.what: the checkpoint to restore, by name

params.name: path
params.what: a checkpoint file kept outside the checkpoints directory

session.restore.answers: `replaying` true means the restore is not finished: the session is rebuilt at zero and set playing towards `target_ms`, which takes the run's own time, so poll `sim.state` until `playing` goes false. A checkpoint taken before the clock moved comes back already there, with `replaying` false. Whatever was loaded before is replaced, seed, frequency and physics included, because a checkpoint restored under other settings is a different study wearing the same name.

example.what: take the session back to a saved moment

session.status.what: report what the session is saying, where the run has got to and which long job is still going, cheaply enough for a script to poll and answered whether or not anything is loaded or drawing
session.status.answers: `jobs` counts only the jobs still running, and `job` is the newest of those: it is absent when nothing is running, which is what a script waiting for a download or a sweep watches for. It carries the job's id, because matching on the wording of a progress line stopped working the moment the wording improved. `status` is the last thing said, replaced while a play is waiting on firmware to come up.

example.what: poll until the work in hand has finished

setup.check.what: what this machine has, what it is missing, and what each one costs
setup.check.answers: Four groups in the order the problems are met - what this build is, what a node would run, what a link is measured over, and what an emulated board needs on top - each row saying its state, what it is for, what it would cost, where it lives and what to do about it, with the verb and parameters that would do it where the application can act. The five counts beside them are those same rows tallied by state, so a script can ask whether anything is wrong without walking the list. Read-only and offline: a check that started a download would be the mistake it exists to report.

example.what: ask whether this machine is ready

sim.faster.what: double how much simulated time one tick covers, trading detail for how long a run takes to watch
sim.faster.answers: `step_ms` is the new tick length. Nothing bounds it: enough calls will step past whole transmissions.

example.what: run twice as coarsely

sim.inject.what: put one packet on the air from a node, to exercise the radio model and the traffic layer without firmware behind it

params.name: node
params.what: which node transmits; absent means the selected one, and a name this network has not got is refused rather than falling through to the first node

sim.inject.answers: Nothing relays what this originates: relaying is a firmware behaviour, and this packet has no firmware behind it.

example.what: transmit from one named node

sim.kind.what: choose whether a run carries real MeshCore firmware or only the channel, and report which it is now

params.name: real
params.what: true to start MeshCore on every node at play; absent leaves the setting alone and only reads it

sim.kind.answers: `running` is how many nodes have firmware up right now, which is not changed by setting `real`: it takes effect at the next play.

example.what: ask what kind of run this is

sim.pause.what: stop the clock where it is, leaving firmware running and the engine built

example.what: hold the run still

sim.play.what: let the clock run, without touching firmware or waiting for the links to be measured
sim.play.answers: `playing` is always true: this verb sets the clock going rather than reporting whether it could.

example.what: start the clock

sim.reset.what: put the clock back to zero and rebuild the engine on the same seed and the same nodes, which is how the arm of a comparison starts
sim.reset.answers: The scenario survives and the run does not: the send schedule is cleared with the clock, and every link is measured again.

example.what: start this scenario over

sim.run.what: play until a stated simulated time and stop there, which is how a script gets a run of a known length instead of watching for one

params.name: for_ms
params.what: simulated milliseconds to run for; anything not a positive number leaves it at ten seconds

sim.run.answers: It returns as soon as the limit is set, not when the run reaches it. Poll `sim.state` until `playing` goes false.

example.what: run for a simulated minute

sim.seed.what: read the seed the run draws its noise and its timing jitter from, or set a new one and rebuild on it

params.name: seed
params.what: the new seed; anything not a positive number reads the current one without changing it

sim.seed.answers: Setting it rebuilds the engine and re-measures every link, so the run starts again rather than continuing on a new draw.

example.what: read the seed this run is on

sim.settle.what: step the engine on a stopped clock so queued serial input reaches the firmware, which is what makes provisioning take effect

params.name: steps
params.what: how many ticks to step; anything not a positive number leaves it at sixty

sim.settle.answers: Refuses with no engine built. It steps synchronously, so it answers only once the steps have been taken.

example.what: let a just-provisioned mesh read what it was sent

sim.slower.what: halve how much simulated time one tick covers
sim.slower.answers: `step_ms` is the new tick length, which reaches zero after enough calls and stops the clock advancing at all.

example.what: run twice as finely

sim.speed.what: set how much simulated time one tick covers, which is the honest form of a speed control

params.name: step_ms
params.what: simulated milliseconds per tick, which is what the engine actually paces on

params.name: factor
params.what: a multiple of ten milliseconds per tick, read only when `step_ms` is absent, for scripts written against the old socket

sim.speed.answers: `step_ms` is what it settled on. Neither parameter positive leaves the tick alone and reports it.

example.what: ten simulated milliseconds a tick

sim.start.what: what a play button presses, which is four different things: it pauses a run already playing, declines while the links are still being measured, brings MeshCore up on every node without playing if this is a firmware run and nothing is up yet, and otherwise starts the clock
sim.start.answers: `playing` is the only key always present. `warming` appears when it declined because the link matrix is not measured yet, and `starting_firmware` when it brought the mesh up instead of playing, which is the case where a second call is needed.

example.what: press play

sim.state.what: report where the run has got to, cheaply enough to poll and safely enough to call before anything is loaded
sim.state.answers: `until_ms` is zero unless `sim.run` set a limit. `events` is the count since the engine was built, not since the last call. The link measurement has three states, not two: `warming` while it runs, `links_measured` once every pair has been walked, and `warm_held` for a warm that stopped to ask permission to download terrain, which is neither. A held warm finishes its own job row, so a wait for the workbench to go idle returns in a moment having waited for nothing - reading that as a measurement is how a study came to be believed over ground nobody fetched. `ground` is what the studies here are standing on, in the shape `terrain.ground` returns.

example.what: ask whether the run has finished

sim.step.what: advance the engine by one tick while the clock is stopped, which is how a paused run is inspected between packets
sim.step.answers: `now_ms` is the simulated clock after the tick. One tick is whatever `sim.speed` last set, not one millisecond.

example.what: move on one tick

sim.toggle.what: play if paused and pause if playing, for a control that is one key
sim.toggle.answers: `playing` is the state it has just moved to, not the one it was in.

example.what: flip the clock

sim.unverified_wiring.what: allow boards whose wiring nobody has watched boot to run anyway, which is the only way a newly imported board is ever verified

params.name: on
params.what: true to lift the gate; absent reads the setting without changing it

sim.unverified_wiring.answers: The setting is saved to preferences, so it outlives the session. Turning it on names the boards it has just trusted.

example.what: ask whether the gate is lifted

study.margin.what: read or set how far outside the study boundary a node still counts, which decides what an imported network keeps

params.name: km
params.what: kilometres beyond the boundary; a negative number is ignored and only reads the current value

example.what: keep nodes up to twenty kilometres outside the boundary

sweep.run.what: push a rising offered load through one node until the network stops carrying what it is given, which is the point a delivery figure taken at one load cannot show
sweep.run.answers: The shape of the plan it has just started, not a result. The plan is fixed and takes no parameters: four message rates from one every two seconds down to one every 250 ms, over six seeds. Those two dozen short simulations run on a worker and the matrix arrives later through an internal callback, with progress under the job id `sweep`. The node swept is the first selected one, or the scenario's first companion where nothing is selected. It refuses where no engine has been built or no node is loaded.

example.what: find where the selected node's mesh saturates

sweep.set.what: take the finished offered-load matrix onto the world, on the one goroutine allowed to apply it
sweep.set.answers: Nothing. It carries a *state.Matrix, which is a Go value nothing outside the process can spell, so anything else is refused rather than applied as an empty matrix.

terrain.allow.what: allow or refuse terrain downloads on this machine, and remember it

params.name: on
params.what: true to download terrain when a study needs it, false to use only what is cached

terrain.allow.answers: `asked` is whether this machine had already answered before the call, never asked being the third state a fresh install is in. `warming` is true where the answer released a measurement that had stopped to ask, because nothing is watching for the answer to arrive and it has to be started again by hand. A refusal releases it as well as a grant: "use only what is cached" is an answer, and a session left held on it never measures a link at all, so the map stays empty and the study that follows has nothing to be honest about.

example.what: let this machine fetch the ground a study needs

terrain.cache.what: say how much memory decoded terrain may occupy, in the unit people think in, and read back where the tiles are kept and whether this machine is allowed to fetch more

params.name: gb
params.what: the ceiling in gigabytes, four thousand-odd tiles to the gigabyte; anything under 0.25 is ignored rather than refused, and absent only reports

terrain.cache.answers: `dir` is where the tiles live on disk, which is permanent: nothing here expires a cached tile. `downloads` is whether terrain may be fetched at all, answered here because this is the verb the interface asks at startup and the switch has to draw its own position on the first frame.

example.what: ask where the terrain is and how much is held

terrain.cache_dir.what: move the terrain cache to another disk, files and all, so a permanent cache that has outgrown where it started does not have to be downloaded again somewhere else

params.name: path
params.what: where the cache should live, created if it is not there already; absent only reports where it lives now, while a path that cannot be written into, one that contains or sits inside the current cache, or a second move while one is still running, is refused rather than queued

terrain.cache_dir.answers: the move runs on a worker with a progress job, so this answers `moving` true before a byte has gone. Asked with no path it answers `dir` instead. A move that fails leaves the cache where it was and says so in the journal.

example.what: put the tiles on the disk with room for them

terrain.cache_moved.what: point the tile store and the settings at the directory a finished move has filled, and say whether the next launch will look there too or download it all again

params.name: dir
params.what: the directory the files were moved to; the callback is refused without it

params.name: files
params.what: how many files moved, for the message; absent counts as none

terrain.ground.what: report what elevation data the current network actually has under it, and whether having none of it was chosen
terrain.ground.answers: `state` is `terrain` where every sampled tile under the network is cached, `partial` where some are, and `bare-earth` where none are. Bare earth is not a missing decoration: the propagation model prices a profile with no elevation as free space, which is the most optimistic answer it has and more optimistic than the best case the rest of the model is documented as. `chosen` says somebody answered the terrain question, either way, so an offline run the operator asked for can be told apart from a fetch that never happened because nobody was asked. `note` is the sentence a study carries in its own result, empty only when the ground is all here. The tile counts are a bounded sample of the study's box rather than a census, so they are there to be compared with each other and not quoted as a size.

example.what: check what the studies here are standing on before believing one

terrain.prefetch.what: download the ground under the loaded network before anything needs it, so the minutes of network time a first measurement would spend invisibly are a visible, priced, stoppable job instead
terrain.prefetch.answers: `tiles` is the area's whole tile count and `to_fetch` how many of them are missing, so `to_fetch` zero means the ground is already cached and nothing was started. Otherwise the download runs as a cancellable job and this returns before it, with `bytes_rough` an average tile size times a count rather than a measurement. Refused where no network is loaded, where the machine has no tile store, and where terrain downloads are switched off, which terrain.allow is what turns on.

example.what: fetch the ground this study stands on

terrain.shade.what: hillshade the relief under one view, which is a tile fetch and a pass over every cell in it, so it runs as a job that says out loud that it is happening

params.name: view
params.what: the borders to shade, as the four numbers south, north, west, east; anything that is not four numbers, and four that are all zero, is refused

terrain.shade.answers: `shading: true` means the job started, not that anything has been drawn. The shading lands later through the internal `terrain.shade_set`, or `terrain.shade_failed` where the view has no elevation to shade.

example.what: shade the relief across Fife

terrain.shade_failed.what: drop the hillshade and say the view has no elevation cached, so a layer that switched on and drew nothing carries its reason

terrain.shade_set.what: hold the finished hillshade, and warn where most of the view was blank ground rather than flat ground
terrain.shade_set.answers: Answers nothing: the shading goes into the snapshot the renderer reads.

tool.set.what: choose what a click on the map does, so a script can place or measure without a hand on the mouse

params.name: name
params.what: select, move, place, link or measure; anything else is refused with that same list

example.what: make the next two clicks a distance

ui.keep_above.what: Say whether a window popped out of the workbench stays above it, and report the setting either way.

params.name: on
params.what: set it; omit to read the current setting without changing it

ui.keep_above.answers: The setting after the call, which is on where nothing has ever chosen: the fault it answers is a panel lost behind the main window. It is a stored preference rather than an act on a window, so it is answered with no interface attached and takes effect on the windows opened after it. It matters on Linux under Wayland, where staying above changes what the window is: our own title bar, no taskbar entry, and a close button that returns the panel to the main window. Elsewhere the platform does it anyway.

example.what: keep a popped-out panel in front of the workbench

ui.said.what: put a line where the operator is already looking, so a script's own step is visible in the status strip and in the session log beside the verbs it drove

params.name: text
params.what: the line to show; anything that is not a bare string or a single-keyed object says an empty line rather than refusing

ui.said.answers: It never refuses, and it does not need an interface: with nothing drawing, the line still goes to the log the session keeps.

example.what: mark a step of a script on screen

ui.scale.what: read or set how large the interface draws itself, the one setting a high-density screen needs and then never again

params.name: scale
params.what: the new scale, one being the interface's own size; absent, zero or negative reads the current scale and changes nothing

ui.scale.answers: The scale in force after the call, read back from the interface rather than repeated from the request, so an interface that clamps it says so. Refuses when no interface is attached.

example.what: make everything a quarter larger on a dense screen

ui.state.what: ask what is on screen for a caller with no eyes: the view, the panels in their own windows, the map tool, and what the run is doing beside them
ui.state.answers: The first four come from whatever is drawing, so another interface may answer with other keys; the rest are the session's own. `jobs` counts the jobs still running and `running` is those same jobs as rows with their ids, because a bare count cannot tell a script what it is waiting for. Refuses when no interface is attached, which is what makes session.status the one to poll.

example.what: check which view a screenshot will catch

update.allow.what: allow or refuse update checks on this machine, and remember it

params.name: on
params.what: true to ask the release page once a day whether a newer release exists, false never to ask

update.allow.answers: `asked` is whether this machine had already answered before the call, never asked being the third state a fresh install is in and the one that spends nothing. Off is the default and stays the default: nothing in the simulation depends on knowing whether a release exists, so a machine with no network, or an operator who does not want the question, loses nothing by never answering it. `checking` is true where the grant started a check straight away, which it does because nothing is watching for permission to arrive and a switch that promises something and does it tomorrow is a switch nobody believes. Allowing a check never downloads anything.

example.what: let this machine find out when a newer release is published

update.check.what: ask the release feed whether a newer release exists
update.check.answers: Starts the check and returns immediately: asking is a network call, and one made on the store's own goroutine would stop the simulation for as long as a socket takes to time out. It announces itself in the jobs strip and the answer lands in `update.status`, which is what a script polls. The routine question is answered by the redirect the releases page already serves - a 302 naming the newest tag, no API call - because GitHub allows an unauthenticated caller 60 requests an hour per address, and an address is a household, an office or an ISP doing carrier-grade NAT; the API is asked once a newer release is found, for the assets and their sizes. A check that could not reach either is an error with a reason, never a report that this build is current: a rate limit, a captive portal and an up-to-date build are three answers and only one of them is about this build. A working copy is refused rather than checked, and says so: a build with no release stamped in it is not behind anything, it is unreleased. Calling this by hand is its own consent for that one check - the preference `update.allow` sets governs the check nobody asked for, the one on a timer.

example.what: find out now whether a newer release has been published

update.checked.what: take a finished check back onto the store's goroutine: publish what the release feed said and say it once
update.checked.answers: Internal: the check reporting back to itself from the worker it runs on. The result it carries is the whole of what `update.status` then answers.

update.download.what: download the release the last check found, beside this build rather than over it
update.download.answers: Refuses unless a check has already found a release this machine could take, and says which of the four reasons applies - nothing has asked yet, the last check could not reach the feed, there is a newer release but nothing published for this platform or this bundle, or this build is already the newest. The fetch runs in the background with its size announced in the jobs strip before it is spent, and it is verified before it is offered: the release publishes SHA256SUMS beside its artefacts, and a file whose digest does not match is deleted rather than kept. That digest comes from the same release as the file, so what it proves is that the download arrived intact; what says the release is ours is the connection to github.com, which is why an asset served from anywhere else is refused outright. Nothing is replaced: the download lands in the update cache and the answer says how to swap it by hand, because a run holds unsaved state and replacing a binary underneath one is a way to lose somebody's work.

example.what: fetch the release the last check found

update.notes.what: open the release page for what the last check found
update.notes.answers: The notes are linked rather than embedded: they are prose, and prose outgrows any panel it is put in. Refuses when no check has named a release page yet.

example.what: read what changed in the release being offered

update.reveal.what: open the folder a downloaded release landed in
update.reveal.answers: Refuses when nothing has been downloaded, because there is then no folder to open. Hands the path to whatever this desktop uses - xdg-open, open, or the Windows file protocol handler - and says so when the machine has none rather than failing silently.

example.what: look at the release that was just downloaded

update.staged.what: take a finished download back onto the store's goroutine: record where it landed and say what to do with it

params.name: path
params.what: where the verified download landed

update.staged.answers: Internal: the download reporting back from the worker it runs on. What it says is the whole instruction for this platform's bundle, including that a client pinned to the old release will be refused by the new workbench.

update.status.what: what the last update check found, without asking anything
update.status.answers: Read-only and offline: every field is empty until something has asked, because nothing here is filled at startup. `newer` is whether a higher release exists at all and `available` is whether one exists that this machine could actually take - they differ where a release is published for platforms this is not one of, or where the package manager owns this copy, and `why` is the reason in words. `artefact` names which bundle this build came out of, because what can honestly be done with a download afterwards differs per bundle. `staged` is where a verified download landed, always beside this build and never on top of it. `error` is why the last check could not answer, which is a different thing from there being nothing newer. `feed` is only set when somebody pointed the check at something other than the published release feed.

example.what: ask whether this build is the newest one, without touching the network

validate.calibrate.what: set the excess path loss term from what the comparison measured, or from a stated figure, and rebuild every link on it

params.name: db
params.what: the excess loss to apply, in decibels, which wins over the measurement; absent uses the measured residual, a negative is refused because excess loss is a loss, and a db that cannot be read as a number is refused rather than falling back to the residual nobody asked for

validate.calibrate.answers: Refuses when nothing has been measured and no db was given: defaulting to 0 dB there is not the absence of calibration but the most optimistic model there is. The figure applied is a total on top of nothing, not a delta, so repeated fetch-then-calibrate rounds converge. It rebuilds the engine and re-measures every link, so `links` is 0 at the moment it answers and fills in as the matrix warms.

example.what: apply a stated excess loss rather than a measured one

validate.compare.what: put what the model predicted beside what was actually heard, and turn the difference into a total excess loss worth applying
validate.compare.answers: A positive `median_db` means the model predicted a stronger signal than was heard, which is the simulator being kinder than the air. `suggested_excess_loss_db` is a total and not a delta: the links these residuals were measured against already carried the current term, so it is that term plus the median. Saturated observations are counted but do not vote. It refuses when nothing matched, and says how much of that was names outside the scenario against pairs with no measured link, because the two want different fixes.

validate.failed.what: take the validation job off the status line and put the reason there instead, so a fetch that matched nothing says which of the several nothings it was

validate.fetch.what: pull what a real deployment actually heard and hand it to the comparison, which is where a number for the excess loss term comes from rather than a guess

params.name: url
params.what: the CoreScope base URL to ask; absent falls back to the source set with import.set_source, and is refused when there is no source either way

params.name: hours
params.what: how far back to ask for, from a minute to a year; absent is a day, and a value outside that range or not a number is refused rather than quietly made a day

validate.fetch.answers: It answers the moment the fetch starts, not with anything fetched. The comparison lands later through the internal `validate.compare`, and every way it can come to nothing - neither endpoint answering, observations carrying keys from another network, no SNR in the window - through `validate.failed` on the status line. This is the one verb here that goes to the network.

example.what: fetch a day of real receptions to compare against

validate.uncalibrate.what: put the excess path loss back to the default, which is a stated guess rather than a measurement, and rebuild every link on it
validate.uncalibrate.answers: The snapshot stops calling itself calibrated, which is the point: the default is a reasonable figure for typical clutter and not this network's. It re-measures the whole link matrix, so the margins move over the seconds after it answers.

example.what: drop a calibration and go back to the stated default

view.delete.what: forget a saved arrangement, deleting the file behind it

params.name: name
params.what: the saved view to remove; one that is not there is refused

view.delete.answers: The layout on screen is not touched: this removes the copy on disk, and nothing is asked first. Refuses when no interface is attached.

example.what: drop a layout that is no longer used

view.list.what: name the saved arrangements there are to load, which is the only way to find out what a machine has kept
view.list.answers: The names alone, sorted, without the .json the files carry. Null where nothing has been saved, and null too where the platform cannot say where config lives, which reads the same from here. Refuses when no interface is attached.

example.what: see which layouts this machine has kept

view.load.what: put a saved arrangement back, windows and all

params.name: name
params.what: the saved view, as view.list names it; one that is not there is refused

view.load.answers: It answers once the arrangement is asked for, the layouts and the view landing on the next frame and the windows opening after that. A file written before docking existed carries no layouts and loads as the declared presets rather than failing. Refuses when no interface is attached.

example.what: go back to the layout a study is read in

view.save.what: keep the arrangement on screen under a name, so a layout built for one kind of work survives the next launch and the next machine

params.name: name
params.what: what to call it; an empty or missing name is refused, and a name already used is overwritten without asking

view.save.answers: It saves every view's arrangement, not only the one on screen, along with which view is showing and which panels are in windows of their own, to a file under the user's config directory. Refuses when no interface is attached.

example.what: keep the layout a coverage study is read in

waterfall.capture.what: take one 200 ms window of what a node's receiver hears and turn it into a spectrogram, of the instant it was asked for rather than of whenever a worker got round to it

params.name: node
params.what: the node to listen at; absent falls back to whichever node is selected, and a name this network has not got is refused rather than read as none

waterfall.capture.answers: `captured` is false without an error whenever there was nothing to draw: no engine, no node selected, or nothing on the air in that instant. Which of the three it was is said on the status line rather than returned.

example.what: look at what one node hears during a flood

window.close.what: close a panel's own window, which returns the panel to the main layout rather than losing it

params.name: name
params.what: the panel whose window is closed; a panel that is not in a window of its own is refused

window.close.answers: Refuses when no interface is attached, and refuses where the interface has no window manager behind it.

example.what: close the window a capture no longer needs

window.open.what: open a panel in a window of its own, the same act as panel.pop_out under the name a caller thinking in windows reaches for

params.name: name
params.what: the panel to give a window; an unknown or missing name is refused with the list of the ones there are

window.open.answers: The window is asked for here and opened by the frame loop, so the answer says it was accepted rather than that a window is up. Refuses when no interface is attached.

example.what: watch the waterfall beside the map

workspace.set.what: Show one of the workbench's top-level views.

params.name: view
params.what: the view's name, as panels.list and the view bar spell it

workspace.set.answers: Refuses when no interface is attached, and refuses a name that is not a view with the list of the ones that are.

example.what: go to the view that asks why one packet failed
